# viz { #wdm.viz }

`viz`

Diagnostic figures.

Design rules followed throughout, and worth stating because they are choices
rather than defaults:

*No dual-axis plots.* Where two quantities of different scale must be shown over
the same period -- prescribed intake and predicted weight, say -- they get
stacked panels sharing an x-axis, never two y-scales on one frame. A dual axis
lets the author place the crossing point anywhere, which makes the visual claim
arbitrary.

*Direct labels on every series.* Colour alone never carries identity. This
matters for color-vision deficiency generally, and specifically because the aqua
series sits below a 3:1 contrast ratio against the surface, so it must be
labelled to be legible at all.

*Recessive chrome.* Gridlines and axes are hairlines in muted ink; the data is
the only thing with weight.

*Uncertainty is drawn, not implied.* Every state estimate is a posterior with a
credible band, and plotting the mean alone would misrepresent how much is
actually known -- particularly for fat mass, whose band is wide enough to be the
main thing worth seeing.

| [plot_innovations](#wdm.viz.plot_innovations) | Standardised one-step-ahead residuals, over time and as a histogram. |
| [plot_intake_log](#wdm.viz.plot_intake_log) | What was actually logged, day by day: intake, macros, fiber, sodium, |
| [plot_maintenance](#wdm.viz.plot_maintenance) | The maintenance estimate as it evolved, against what was eaten. |
| [plot_parameter_evolution](#wdm.viz.plot_parameter_evolution) | What the filter believed about each parameter, day by day. |
| [plot_parameters](#wdm.viz.plot_parameters) | Posterior medians and 90 % intervals, normalized to the prior center. |

### mdates_num { #wdm.viz.mdates_num }

```python
viz.mdates_num(x)
```

A plotted x value (date or number) in matplotlib's internal units.

### plot_composition { #wdm.viz.plot_composition }

```python
viz.plot_composition(fit_episode, *, path=None)
```

Fat and lean mass over time, with bands.

Worth reading with the bands rather than the lines. Fat mass is only weakly
identified from scale data -- it enters the dynamics solely through the
effective energy density -- so its interval is wide, and a narrow reading of
the mean would be overclaiming.

### plot_innovations { #wdm.viz.plot_innovations }

```python
viz.plot_innovations(fit_episode, *, path=None)
```

Standardised one-step-ahead residuals, over time and as a histogram.

The primary check that the model is adequate. If it is, these are white noise
with unit variance. Structure in the left panel means the dynamics are
missing something; a histogram wider than the reference curve means the noise
model is understated, which shows up downstream as overconfident intervals.

### plot_intake_log { #wdm.viz.plot_intake_log }

```python
viz.plot_intake_log(episode, *, steps=None, path=None)
```

What was actually logged, day by day: intake, macros, fiber, sodium,
exercise, steps.

Unlike the other figures here, this one plots inputs rather than filtered
state -- there is no estimation to distrust, only gaps to be honest about.
Days without a food log are left as gaps rather than the reference values
the model substitutes internally (`~wdm.io.Episode` fills unknown
carbohydrate and sodium with the reference intake, habitual eating, so the
water states have something to condition on); plotting those fill values here would make
logging coverage look better than it is. Exercise is the one series where
zero *is* the honest default for an unlogged day, per ``Episode``'s own
convention, and steps -- not part of the model at all -- are passed in
separately from the raw CSV.

### plot_maintenance { #wdm.viz.plot_maintenance }

```python
viz.plot_maintenance(
    fit,
    fit_episode,
    episode,
    *,
    path=None,
    n_samples=2000,
    seed=0,
)
```

The maintenance estimate as it evolved, against what was eaten.

Maintenance here is the non-adaptive expenditure at each day's trend weight,
``c0 + c1 W``, under that day's filtered belief about the two coefficients.
The band comes from sampling their joint filtered distribution: the two are
strongly correlated, so their sum is far better known than either, and
adding marginal variances would overstate the band. The logged intake on the
same axis makes the deficit visible directly; both are kcal/day, so one
axis is honest.

### plot_parameter_evolution { #wdm.viz.plot_parameter_evolution }

```python
viz.plot_parameter_evolution(fit, fit_episode, *, path=None)
```

What the filter believed about each parameter, day by day.

The filtered (not smoothed) estimate: each day shows only what the record up
to that morning implied, so the panels replay how the evidence accumulated.
Values are relative to the prior center, as in `plot_parameters`; a
band that stays as wide as it started has learned nothing, whatever its
median does. Small multiples rather than one crowded frame, since the nine
parameters share no scale and need no comparison by color.

### plot_parameters { #wdm.viz.plot_parameters }

```python
viz.plot_parameters(fit, *, path=None)
```

Posterior medians and 90 % intervals, normalized to the prior center.

Normalising is what makes the figure readable: the parameters span nine
orders of magnitude in natural units, and the interesting question is not
their absolute values but whether the data moved them off the prior at all.
A point sitting on the dashed line with a wide interval learned nothing.

### plot_plan { #wdm.viz.plot_plan }

```python
viz.plot_plan(plan, *, fit_episode=None, episode=None, max_days=28, path=None)
```

Prescribed intake and predicted weight, as stacked panels.

Two panels rather than two y-axes. Intake is in kilocalories and weight in
pounds; overlaying them on a shared frame would require choosing where the
two scales cross, and that choice would silently determine which of the two
"leads" the other.

``max_days`` caps how much of the plan is drawn, independent of how long a
horizon it was actually solved over. Deadline-mode plans can span months;
plotting all of it would swamp the readable near-term detail with a long,
increasingly speculative tail, when only the first stretch is close to
being acted on. ``None`` plots the whole thing.

The weight panel is future-only -- just the optimizer's horizon -- unless
``fit_episode`` is given, in which case the filtered scale/tissue trend
leading up to today is drawn in the same two series, distinguished from the
plan only by a lower alpha and a "today" marker. Without that context a
plan reads as an isolated, disconnected forecast; with it, the plan reads
as a continuation of where you actually are. ``episode`` adds the raw
weigh-ins the trend was fitted to, when available.

### plot_plan_vs_actual { #wdm.viz.plot_plan_vs_actual }

```python
viz.plot_plan_vs_actual(log_rows, episode, *, path=None)
```

Each day's prescription, from the plans log, against what was eaten.

``log_rows`` are the rows of ``plans/log.csv``; a day's prescription is the
last plan logged with that start date, the one ``wdm log`` compares against.

### plot_trajectory { #wdm.viz.plot_trajectory }

```python
viz.plot_trajectory(
    fit_episode,
    episode,
    *,
    path=None,
    title='Weight trajectory',
)
```

Raw weigh-ins, the smoothed trend, and its credible band.

The single most useful figure here. The raw points scatter by a pound or more
day to day; the trend line is what actually moved. Seeing both together is
the whole argument for filtering.
